## ✨ Highlights

- 🔑 **Single sign-on for the Controller**: accounts sign in through an OpenID Connect provider - Keycloak, a Synology's SSO Server, Authentik, any other. The provider's groups decide each person's role, the account is made at its first sign-in, and signing out of the Controller signs out of the provider too where it says how. The password form stays. Every build signs in through a real Keycloak.

## 🖥️ Controller

- **Single sign-on through OpenID Connect** ([#228](https://github.com/swenske/Janus/pull/228), [the guide](https://janus.sw-servers.net/docs/guide/sso.md)) - **Accounts** tab › **Single sign-on**:
  - **A provider**: presets for Keycloak (the Group Membership mapper's `/full/paths`), a Synology's SSO Server (its `username` claim, the `groups` scope, no `profile`) and any other; the redirect and post-logout URIs to register there, for the Controller as you opened it; the client secret, write-only and sealed with the master key; how its certificate is trusted (the system's store, a CA, a fingerprint); and **Test**, which fetches its discovery and keys the way a sign-in will and says what won't work.
  - **Rules**: a group gives a role over everything, or a grant on the nodes some labels pick, narrowed to some domains. The highest role wins; nobody a rule doesn't match gets in, unless the provider has a default role.
  - **Accounts it makes**, at their first sign-in, named after the provider's username: no password; their role is what the rules give their groups - at every sign-in, and at once when the rules change. They lapse a week (by default) after their last sign-in through the provider - their sessions, API tokens and SSH keys with them -, so someone removed there loses everything the Controller gave them.
  - **An account with a password** links its identity from **Your account** (its password again; the provider asks to sign in), and keeps its own role. A name a local account has is never taken over.
  - **The second factor**: the Controller's own by default, as for a password - or the provider's, trusted as is or only when its ID token carries the `acr` or `amr` you name (Keycloak's levels of authentication, its AMR mapper).
  - **Signing out** goes through the provider's sign-out (Keycloak), or stays local when it has none (a Synology).
  - **How it's checked**: the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), a state and a nonce; the ID token's issuer exactly the provider's, its audience, expiry and signature (asymmetric algorithms only), its nonce, `azp` and `at_hash`; an identity bound to its account by issuer and subject, never by a name or an e-mail address. A failed sign-in shows a reference; the Controller's log says more under it, and names the claims a provider's ID token carried (never their values) at its first sign-in after a change.
  - `janusctl login` through the browser works for any account: sign in through the provider on the page it opens.
- **The last enabled admin who signs in with a password** can't be demoted, disabled or deleted: the admins a provider makes don't count - the password form is the way in when no provider is.
- **A Traffic flow too tall for the window** ([#227](https://github.com/swenske/Janus/pull/227)) stays at 75 % of it, not twice its height.

## 🧪 Tests and tooling

- **A real Keycloak signs in to the Controller** (`make controller-sso-test`, in the image build's Controller job): Keycloak 26.8.1, pinned by digest, and the Controller on a private network under two names - two sites, as in real life -, headless Chromium signing in through Keycloak's own pages: roles from groups, refusals, janusctl's sign-in page kept across the round trip, signing out of Keycloak, linking, a group changed in Keycloak, the rules changed on the Controller, Keycloak's second factor counted, a provider disabled and removed - no page error, no CSP report, axe on every page.
- One new Go module: `github.com/coreos/go-oidc/v3` 3.20.0.

## ⚠️ Upgrade notes

- **The Controller**: update it from its page, as usual. Nothing changes until an admin adds a provider.
- **Nodes**: nothing changed since v2026.10.22 but the version - updating them is optional.
- **Adding a provider**: open the Controller by the name your users will use - the provider sends the browser back to exactly that address, and a Synology refuses an IP address.
- **Going back to an older Controller** after accounts signed in through a provider: an older version drops the identities and which provider made an account when it saves the accounts. Those accounts then have no password and no identity - `dashboardd reset-user NAME` gives one a password.
